docTitle: A 4-step system to remember the books you read for work

slides.title:
Remember
*what* you
read for
*work.*
slides.sub: A 4-step system for non-fiction. A few minutes per book.

slides.body: Weeks after finishing a book for work or study, you can give the gist and one or two points. Not the argument.
slides.punch:
You keep a _feeling_ about the book,
not the book itself.

slides.title:
Ideas stick when they
have a place to *go.*

rows.b: You know which part it belongs to.
Each idea has somewhere to go.

slides.title: Decode the title.
slides.meaning: A term from philosopher Ivan Illich: tools that give power back to the person using them.
slides.guess: My guess before page one: it argues research tools should be usable by ordinary people, not just experts.
slides.lede:
Example: _Convivial Toolbox_.
Look up the word you don’t know.

slides.title: Map the contents.
slides.lede: Chapters, sub-headings, even page counts. Then group them into blocks.
slides.takeaway: A manual _masquerading_ as a textbook: the theory up front is there to make the tools make sense.

slides.title: Memorise it.
slides.lede: Learn the chapter titles by heart. Sub-headings too, if you can.
slides.quote: Skimming the headings helps. Memorising them sticks: it makes the map stronger in my mind.
slides.note: An old idea: Mortimer Adler’s inspectional reading (_How to Read a Book_, 1940). Others call it priming.

slides.title:
Guess, then read
to check.
questions: Where and when does bridging happen?
What are the ways we can bridge the gap?
slides.takeaway: My guess: a “gap” problem sits at the heart of this book. So when “gap” turns up early, I’ll notice. Read cold, I’d have missed it.

slides.title:
Where it
pays *off.*

rows.head: Thesis and research
rows.sub: Dense sources you’ll cite or build on.

rows.head: Textbooks and manuals
rows.sub: Anything with a real contents page.

rows.head: Books you’ll have to explain
rows.sub: When someone asks what it was about.

slides.note: Skip it for fiction. With a novel, not knowing what comes next is the point.

slides.title:
Before you read
a book for work

rows.head: Decode the title.
rows.sub: What is it already telling you?

rows.head: Memorise it.
rows.sub: If you can. Then every new idea has a place.

rows.head: Guess, then check.
rows.sub: Read to find out: right or wrong?

slides.corner: // save it for your next book
slides.title:
Try it on
your next
*book.*
